Mixed models with brsmm

Source: vignettes/brs-mm.Rmd
brs-mm.Rmd

brsmm() adds Gaussian random effects to the mean submodel of brs() for clustered or longitudinal scores (patients with repeated visits, raters, centers). This vignette covers the model, the integration methods, random-effect summaries and tests, marginal and conditional predictions, residuals, group-level cross-validation and simulation. The interval-censored likelihood and the interval maps are those of vignette("brs-intro"). The data sets are small so that the vignette builds quickly; the results are illustrative.

library(betaregscale)

The model

For observation ii of group gg, g1(μgi)=xgi⊤β+wgi⊤bg,g2(σgi)=zgi⊤γ,bg∼N(0,D), g_1(\mu_{gi}) = x_{gi}^\top \beta + w_{gi}^\top b_g, \qquad g_2(\sigma_{gi}) = z_{gi}^\top \gamma, \qquad b_g \sim N(0, D), where wgiw_{gi} is the row of the random-effects design given by random = ~ terms | group (~ 1 | id for a random intercept, ~ 1 + x | id for an intercept and a slope with a free correlation). The dispersion submodel has no random effects. Given bgb_g, each score contributes the cell probability of brs(), and the marginal log-likelihood is ℓ(θ)=∑glog⁡∫∏iP(Sgi=sgi∣b)φ(b;0,D)db. \ell(\theta) = \sum_g \log \int \prod_i P(S_{gi} = s_{gi} \mid b)\, \varphi(b; 0, D)\, db . D=LL⊤D = LL^\top is parameterized by its lower Cholesky factor: the log of each diagonal entry and the off-diagonal entries. These are the (re_chol_logsd)_ and (re_chol)_ entries of coef(); for a random intercept the single entry is log⁡SD(b)\log \mathrm{SD}(b).

Integration methods

The integral is computed around the mode b̂g\hat b_g of the log integrand, with curvature HgH_g there:

  • int_method = "laplace" (default): the Laplace approximation, fast and accurate when groups are not tiny.
  • int_method = "aghq": adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature with n_points nodes per dimension (default 11) on a product grid centered at b̂g\hat b_g and scaled by Hg−1/2H_g^{-1/2} (at most 500000 nodes).
  • int_method = "qmc": importance sampling from N(b̂g,Hg−1)N(\hat b_g, H_g^{-1}) on qmc_points Halton points (default 1024). It is deterministic and, with two or more random effects, slightly underestimates the log-likelihood; prefer "aghq" for up to three random effects.

optim() uses the compiled gradient of the chosen approximation; the Hessian for vcov() is a central difference of that gradient.

Simulated data

brsmm_sim() simulates scores from this model, given the random-effect standard deviations and correlation. Here: 30 patients with four visits on an NRS-11 scale, a centered time tc, a treatment arm trt, and a random intercept and time slope:

d <- expand.grid(visit = 1:4, id = 1:30)
d$tc <- (d$visit - 2.5) / 1.5
d$trt <- as.integer(d$id %% 2 == 0)
set.seed(7)
s <- brsmm_sim(~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 + tc | id, data = d,
               beta = c(-0.3, -0.4, -0.5), phi = qlogis(0.15),
               re_sd = c(0.8, 0.3), re_cor = 0.3, ncuts = 10)
head(s)
#>      left right    yt y delta visit id         tc trt
#> 1 0.85000  0.95 9e-01 9     3     1  1 -1.0000000   0
#> 2 0.85000  0.95 9e-01 9     3     2  1 -0.3333333   0
#> 3 0.55000  0.65 6e-01 6     3     3  1  0.3333333   0
#> 4 0.55000  0.65 6e-01 6     3     4  1  1.0000000   0
#> 5 0.25000  0.35 3e-01 3     3     1  2 -1.0000000   1
#> 6 0.00001  0.05 1e-05 0     1     2  2 -0.3333333   1
attr(s, "truth")$par
#>                    (Intercept)                             tc 
#>                     -0.3000000                     -0.4000000 
#>                            trt              (phi)_(Intercept) 
#>                     -0.5000000                     -1.7346011 
#> (re_chol_logsd)_(Intercept)|id    (re_chol)_tc:(Intercept)|id 
#>                     -0.2231436                      0.0900000 
#>          (re_chol_logsd)_tc|id 
#>                     -1.2511281

The attribute "truth" holds the true parameters in the order and on the scale of coef(), and "ranef" the simulated random effects.

Fitting 

fit_ri <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s)
fit_rs <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 + tc | id, data = s)
summary(fit_rs)
#> 
#> Call:
#> brsmm(formula = y ~ tc + trt, random = ~1 + tc | id, data = s)

The random-effects block reports the standard deviations and the correlation with intervals built on the log scale (SD) and the atanh\mathrm{atanh} scale (correlation) and mapped back. It gives no zz-test: a variance of zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so test it with anova() (below). The same numbers are in summary(fit)$varcorr.

The three integration methods give nearly the same estimates on this data:

fit_aghq <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s,
                  int_method = "aghq", n_points = 7)
fit_qmc <- brsmm(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s,
                 int_method = "qmc", qmc_points = 256)
round(cbind(laplace = c(coef(fit_ri), logLik = logLik(fit_ri)),
            aghq = c(coef(fit_aghq), logLik = logLik(fit_aghq)),
            qmc = c(coef(fit_qmc), logLik = logLik(fit_qmc))), 4)
#>                                  laplace      aghq       qmc
#> (Intercept)                       0.0744    0.0751    0.0741
#> tc                               -0.3611   -0.3599   -0.3602
#> trt                              -0.7140   -0.7163   -0.7160
#> (phi)_(Intercept)                -1.7110   -1.7104   -1.7100
#> (re_chol_logsd)_(Intercept)|id    0.0545    0.0665    0.0641
#> logLik                         -253.9230 -253.3591 -253.4076

Random effects

ranef() returns the conditional modes b̂g\hat b_g, one row per group; fit$random$D and fit$random$sd_b hold the estimated covariance matrix and standard deviations:

head(ranef(fit_rs))
#>   (Intercept)           tc
#> 1   0.8194782 -0.029209222
#> 2  -1.5034029 -0.100498130
#> 3  -1.5294370 -0.087103237
#> 4  -0.5462813 -0.002064520
#> 5  -0.7803565 -0.001166132
#> 6  -0.9184533 -0.055430537
fit_rs$random$D
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] 1.14198316 0.03463383
#> [2,] 0.03463383 0.03881125

brsmm_re_study() summarizes the random effects: the covariance, the shrinkage of the modes and the intraclass correlation of logit(Y)\mathrm{logit}(Y), computed with the beta level-1 variance:

brsmm_re_study(fit_rs)
#> 
#> Random-effects study
#> Groups: 30 
#> 
#> Random-effects (VarCorr):
#>   Name                      Std.Dev.  Corr
#>   (Intercept)                 1.0686
#>   tc                          0.1970  0.1645
#> 
#> ICC (logit(Y) scale, beta level-1 variance): 0.5704
#> 
#> Summary by term (SD_model = model SD; shrinkage = Var(modes)/Var(model)):
#>         term sd_model mean_mode sd_mode shrinkage_ratio shapiro_p
#>  (Intercept)   1.0686    0.0138  0.9665          0.8179    0.6541
#>           tc   0.1970    0.0026  0.0725          0.1354    0.7503
autoplot.brsmm(fit_rs, type = "ranef_caterpillar")

autoplot.brsmm() also draws "ranef_density", "ranef_pairs", "ranef_qq", "shrinkage", "calibration", "score_dist" and "residuals_by_group"; plot.brsmm() gives the panels of plot.brs() with response or Pearson residuals, plus random-effect panels.

Testing variance components

Adding a random-effect term puts its variance on the boundary of the parameter space under the null hypothesis, so the likelihood ratio does not follow χd2\chi^2_d. When a model adds one random-effect term, anova() uses the mixture 12χd−12+12χd2\frac12\chi^2_{d-1} + \frac12\chi^2_d (Self and Liang, 1987; Stram and Lee, 1994): 12χ02+12χ12\frac12\chi^2_0 + \frac12\chi^2_1 from brs() to a random intercept, and 12χ12+12χ22\frac12\chi^2_1 + \frac12\chi^2_2 from a random intercept to an intercept and slope. The heading of the table says which rows use it.

fit_0 <- brs(y ~ tc + trt, data = s)
anova(fit_0, fit_ri, fit_rs)
#> Likelihood-ratio comparison of brs/brsmm models
#> Rows M2, M3: one added random effect (variance on the boundary); Pr(>Chisq) from the chi-bar-square mixture 1/2 chi2(Df - 1) + 1/2 chi2(Df).
#> 
#>            Df  logLik    AIC    BIC   Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)    
#> M1 (brs)    4 -279.98 567.97 579.12                              
#> M2 (brsmm)  5 -253.92 517.85 531.78 52.1196      1  2.611e-13 ***
#> M3 (brsmm)  7 -253.85 521.69 541.21  0.1517      2     0.8119    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

When a variance is essentially zero, brsmm() warns “Variance component at the boundary”; rely on the likelihood-ratio test for that term.

AIC() and BIC() accept several fits, brs and brsmm alike, and return a df/criterion table as stats::AIC() and stats::BIC() do. There is no single sample size for a mixed model: BIC() counts observations by default and groups with n = "groups". Compare BIC values only under the same convention.

AIC(fit_0, fit_ri, fit_rs)
#>        df      AIC
#> fit_0   4 567.9655
#> fit_ri  5 517.8459
#> fit_rs  7 521.6942
BIC(fit_ri, fit_rs)
#>        df      BIC
#> fit_ri  5 531.7834
#> fit_rs  7 541.2066
BIC(fit_ri, fit_rs, n = "groups")
#>        df      BIC
#> fit_ri  5 524.8519
#> fit_rs  7 531.5026

Conditional and marginal predictions

predict() gives conditional quantities: a group of the fit uses its mode b̂g\hat b_g, a new group gets b=0b = 0:

nd <- data.frame(tc = 0, trt = 1, id = c(1, 999))
predict(fit_ri, newdata = nd, type = "expected_score")
#> [1] 5.448165 3.453218

Under a nonlinear link, the prediction at b=0b = 0 describes a subject whose random effects are zero, which is not the population average. brs_marginal() integrates the random effects out to give population-averaged score probabilities, expected scores and exceedance probabilities P(S≥k)P(S \ge k), with delta-method standard errors over all parameters; conditional = TRUE sets b=0b = 0 instead. The grouping variable is not needed in newdata:

nd <- data.frame(tc = c(-1, 1), trt = 1)
brs_marginal(fit_ri, nd, type = "expected_score")
#>   tc trt row estimate std.error    lower    upper
#> 1 -1   1   1 4.433166 0.6380772 3.242149 5.693117
#> 2  1   1   2 3.048002 0.5686567 2.057841 4.259101
brs_marginal(fit_ri, nd, type = "expected_score", conditional = TRUE)
#>   tc trt row estimate std.error    lower    upper
#> 1 -1   1   1 4.308536 0.7745230 2.895803 5.843569
#> 2  1   1   2 2.684320 0.6323208 1.633255 4.081798

Differences between rows, such as the change from the first to the last visit in P(S≥5)P(S \ge 5), are given by contrast:

brs_marginal(fit_ri, nd, type = "exceed", k = 5, contrast = c(2, 1))
#>   contrast row1 row2 k   estimate  std.error      lower       upper
#> 1    2 - 1    2    1 5 -0.1981716 0.06312098 -0.3218864 -0.07445672

Residuals

For type = "rqr" (randomized quantile residuals) and "cell_deviance", re selects how the random effects enter:

  • "conditional" (default): at the modes b̂g\hat b_g. The modes are shrunk toward zero, so the rqr residuals are not exactly N(0,1)N(0, 1) under the model, especially for small groups.
  • "marginal": from the marginal distribution of each observation, with the random effects integrated out. The rqr residuals are N(0,1)N(0, 1) under the model; residuals of the same group are correlated.
  • "posterior": at one draw of each bgb_g from its posterior (importance resampling with n_draws proposals per group, default 200). The rqr residuals are close to independent N(0,1)N(0, 1) under the model, without the shrinkage of the modes.
set.seed(1)
res <- sapply(c("conditional", "marginal", "posterior"), function(r)
  residuals(fit_ri, type = "rqr", re = r))
round(rbind(mean = colMeans(res), sd = apply(res, 2, sd)), 3)
#>      conditional marginal posterior
#> mean      -0.013    0.007     0.003
#> sd         0.883    1.019     0.999

The other types of residuals.brs() ("response", "pearson", …) are evaluated at the conditional modes.

Group-level cross-validation

brsmm_cv() forms folds by group, so all observations of a group are held out together. Each held-out group is scored by its marginal log-likelihood at the training estimates: its random effects are integrated out, so no estimate of them is needed. seed makes the folds reproducible, and attr(, "folds") returns them for reuse with another model:

cv_ri <- brsmm_cv(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 | id, data = s, k = 3, seed = 1)
cv_ri
#>   repeat fold n_groups_train n_groups_test n_train n_test log_score converged
#> 1      1    1             20            10      80     40 -84.01975      TRUE
#> 2      1    2             20            10      80     40 -85.92605      TRUE
#> 3      1    3             20            10      80     40 -87.83580      TRUE
#>   error warning
#> 1  <NA>    <NA>
#> 2  <NA>    <NA>
#> 3  <NA>    <NA>
folds <- attr(cv_ri, "folds")[[1]]
cv_rs <- brsmm_cv(y ~ tc + trt, random = ~ 1 + tc | id, data = s,
                  folds = folds)
c(ri = attr(cv_ri, "log_score"), rs = attr(cv_rs, "log_score"))
#>        ri        rs 
#> -257.7816 -259.1025

The total held-out log score is the log probability of the held-out scores (higher is better). For score data it is on the same scale as the held-out log-likelihood of any other model that gives a pmf on 0,…,K0, \ldots, K, evaluated on the same folds. brs_loglik_contrib() returns the per-group contributions of a fit, also for new data.

Simulation from a fit

simulate() draws new scores from a fitted model. For brsmm fits, re = "marginal" (default) draws new random effects and re = "conditional" keeps the conditional modes. A quick check compares the observed share of each border score with its simulated distribution:

sims <- simulate(fit_ri, nsim = 50, seed = 1)
obs <- c(p0 = mean(s$y == 0), p10 = mean(s$y == 10))
sim_p <- rbind(p0 = colMeans(sims == 0), p10 = colMeans(sims == 10))
cbind(observed = obs, t(apply(sim_p, 1, quantile, c(0.05, 0.95))))
#>       observed          5%       95%
#> p0  0.08333333 0.041666667 0.1333333
#> p10 0.06666667 0.008333333 0.0675000

Boundary cutpoints

cutpoints = "boundary" works in brsmm() as in brs() (see vignette("brs-intro")), with the same requirements and the same 2-df likelihood-ratio test against the fixed map; brsmm_sim() simulates from given boundary cutpoints.

  • Pinheiro, J. C., and Bates, D. M. (1995). Approximations to the log-likelihood function in the nonlinear mixed-effects model. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 4(1), 12–35. https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.1995.10474663
  • Self, S. G., and Liang, K.-Y. (1987). Asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators and likelihood ratio tests under nonstandard conditions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(398), 605–610.
  • Stram, D. O., and Lee, J. W. (1994). Variance components testing in the longitudinal mixed effects model. Biometrics, 50(4), 1171–1177.
